• For related work and baselines:

• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current state-of-the-art methods for detecting Machine-Generated Text (MGT) often rely on non-parametric "two-sample tests." These methods operate on a rigid assumption: that Human-Written Texts (HWT) follow a specific, known distribution, and any text deviating from this distribution is automatically classified as machine-generated.

This approach creates a critical flaw in real-world scenarios. It fails to account for the natural diversity of human writing. If a human writes a text that is stylistically unique or deviates from the reference examples (out-of-distribution), these detectors frequently flag it as artificial. This results in an unacceptably high False Positive Rate (FPR), which poses significant ethical risks in sensitive applications like academic integrity verification, where falsely accusing a human of using AI can have severe consequences.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can significantly reduce false positives by reframing the detection task. Instead of asking, "Does this text belong to the human distribution?" (a binary inclusion/exclusion decision), we propose asking, "Is this text *statistically closer* to the human distribution or the machine distribution?"

By treating detection as a **Relative Test** rather than a standard two-sample test, we acknowledge that human and machine text distributions may overlap. We posit that a comparative approach—measuring relative similarity to unauthored text against both human and machine reference sets—will provide a more robust decision boundary. Furthermore, we hypothesize that the kernel function used to measure these similarities can be optimized via deep learning to maximize the distinguishability between the two categories.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to develop a non-parametric detection framework titled **R-Detect**, utilizing a Deep Kernel Relative Test.

**1. Data Representation and Reference Sets**
We will maintain two reference pools: a set of known Human-Written Texts and a set of known Machine-Generated Texts. When a new, unauthored "Query" text arrives, we will use a fixed feature extractor (such as a pre-trained language model) to convert all texts into high-dimensional vector representations.

**2. Deep Kernel Optimization**
Standard kernels (like Gaussian kernels) measure similarity based on fixed geometric properties. We propose to learn a "Deep Kernel"—a neural network-based transformation designed to map text representations into a space where the statistical difference between human and machine text is maximized. We will train this component by maximizing the test power of a two-sample test on our reference datasets, effectively "teaching" the kernel what features distinguish human writing from AI generation.

**3. Relative Testing Mechanism**
Once the kernel is optimized, the detection process will follow this logical flow:
*   Calculate the distributional discrepancy (similarity score) between the Query text and the Human Reference set.
*   Calculate the distributional discrepancy between the Query text and the Machine Reference set.
*   Apply a statistical hypothesis test to determine if the Query is significantly closer to one reference set than the other.

**4. Decision Rule**
Unlike previous methods that reject a null hypothesis if the text is "different from human," our method will only flag a text as MGT if the statistical test confirms it is significantly closer to the machine distribution than the human distribution. If the result is ambiguous or the text is equidistant, the system defaults to assuming human authorship, thereby preserving innocence in uncertain cases.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Paradigm Shift:** We aim to move the field from "anomaly detection" (is this different from human?) to "comparative verification" (which source does this resemble more?), providing a more logical framework for the era of advanced LLMs.
*   **Reduced False Positives:** We expect this method to drastically lower the rate at which unique human writing is misclassified as AI, addressing a primary ethical concern in current detectors.
*   **Agility and Interpretability:** As a non-parametric approach, this method will not require training a classifier on every new LLM release. It relies on comparing distributions, making it adaptable to new models simply by updating the reference pool.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive experimental framework to evaluate the performance of the proposed "R-Detect" method (Deep Kernel Relative Test) against state-of-the-art baselines for Machine-Generated Text (MGT) detection.

*   **Problem Formulation:** We treated MGT detection as a relative hypothesis testing problem to determine if a text sample is statistically closer to the distribution of Human-Written Texts (HWTs) or MGTs, rather than assuming it belongs exclusively to one or the other (as in two-sample tests).
*   **Feature Extraction:**
    *   Default: OpenAI’s RoBERTa-based GPT-2 detector model (last hidden state, dimension 768).
    *   Alternative extractors tested: Falcon-RW-1b, RoBERTa-base, ChatGPT-detector-RoBERTa.
    *   Input handling: Max 100 tokens per sentence for the kernel network.
*   **Deep Kernel Architecture:**
    *   Network $\phi$: Hidden-layer transformer followed by a projector (768 $\to$ 512 dimensions) and a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) (51,200 $\to$ 300 dimensions).
    *   Optimization: We maximized the test power of the two-sample test (2ST) to learn the kernel parameters.
    *   Optimizer: Adam optimizer.
    *   Hyperparameters: Learning rate $= 0.00005$, Batch size $= 200$, $\lambda = 10^{-8}$.
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Test Power on MGT ($tp^{MGT}$):** Equivalent to True Positive Rate (TPR). Higher is better.
    *   **Test Power on HWT ($tp^{HWT}$):** Equivalent to False Positive Rate (FPR). Lower is better.
    *   **AUROC:** Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve.
    *   **Running Time:** Measured in seconds.
*   **Datasets:**
    *   **HC3 (Human ChatGPT Comparison Corpus):** 24,321 paired answers. Used for training kernels and "Seen HWT" distribution tests.
    *   **TruthfulQA (TQA):** 817 questions/answers (Human, ChatGPT, GPT-4). Used for "Unseen HWT" distribution tests.
    *   **RAID:** Over 6 million generations across 11 models, 8 domains, and 11 adversarial attacks. Used for English and Non-English robustness tests.
    *   **DetectRL:** 100,800 human samples and 134,400 MGT samples (including prompt and paraphrase attacks).
    *   **Essay Dataset:** 5 random human essays rewritten by GPT-4o using the prompt "rewrite".
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Non-Parametric:**
        *   R-Detect-km: R-Detect with Gaussian kernel (median heuristic bandwidth).
        *   R-Detect w/o k*: R-Detect with Gaussian kernel ($\sigma=1$).
        *   MPP-HWT: Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) test using HWT as reference.
        *   MPP-MGT: MMD test using MGT as reference.
        *   MPP-R: Combined MPP using both references, selecting the smaller p-value.
    *   **Parametric:**
        *   DetectGPT, Radar, Fast-DetectGPT, DNA-GPT, DALD, Text-Fluoroscopy.
        *   Bino: Binoculars method (threshold 0.5).
        *   Bino-FPR: Binoculars method (low FPR threshold ~0.85).
*   **Experimental Configurations:**
    *   **Significance Level ($\alpha$):** Default 0.05; also tested 0.90.
    *   **Token Sizes:** 512 (default) and 256.
    *   **Reference Data:** Randomly sampled from the respective dataset splits (e.g., remaining HC3 data).
    *   **Replication:** Experiments were repeated $10 \times 10$ times (10 rounds, 10 shuffles per round).
    *   **Hardware:** Intel Core i9 14900K and NVIDIA RTX 4090.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Observation 1 (Relative Test Mechanism):** By utilizing unauthored text as a reference in a relative test framework, we determined whether a target text's distribution was statistically closer to HWT or MGT. This approach avoided the "exclusive" assumption (that a text must belong solely to HWT or MGT) inherent in two-sample tests, effectively reducing false positives in cases of distribution overlap.
*   **Observation 2 (Decision Score Separability):** Our analysis of decision scores revealed that R-Detect (using $1 - p$-value) yielded scores consistently close to 0 for HWT and close to 1 for MGT. In contrast, the baseline Bino produced scores for HWT and MGT that were spatially closer, making the detection highly sensitive to threshold selection.
*   **Observation 3 (Robustness to Thresholds):** R-Detect demonstrated robust performance across a wide range of significance thresholds ($\alpha$) from 0.05 to 0.9. Conversely, the Bino baseline required a precise threshold window (0.85–0.90) to function correctly; thresholds outside this range resulted in complete failure (either high FPR or low TPR).
*   **Observation 4 (GPT-4 Rewritten Texts):** In scenarios where GPT-4o rewrote human essays, R-Detect maintained a distinct "green zone" of valid thresholds that balanced TPR and FPR. The parametric baseline (Bino) failed to find such a threshold, performing no better than random guessing on these challenging samples.
*   **Observation 5 (Cross-Distribution Generalization):** While baseline non-parametric methods (MPP-HWT/MGT) adapted to new LLMs (e.g., training on HC3, testing on TQA-GPT4), they suffered from high False Positive Rates when the HWT distribution changed (seen vs. unseen). R-Detect maintained high detection accuracy and low FPR across both seen (HC3) and unseen (TQA) HWT distributions.
*   **Observation 6 (Efficiency):** In terms of computational efficiency, R-Detect ran significantly faster than the Bino baseline (180.25s vs 1064.36s in Table 4 comparisons).
*   **Observation 7 (Non-English & Optimizations):** While zero-shot performance on non-English texts was suboptimal, optimizing the kernel and using appropriate reference data (from the target language) dramatically improved R-Detect's AUROC (e.g., improving from 0.3048 to 0.9490 on N/E mix1).

references.text:
## Problem Statement

The proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has necessitated reliable methods for Machine-Generated Text (MGT) detection. Existing post-hoc detectors largely fall into parametric categories (classifier-based or metric-based), which are brittle; their performance degrades significantly when the specific generation mechanism changes or when facing unseen LLMs.

While non-parametric methods, specifically those based on the **Kernel Two-Sample Test (2ST)**, offer superior adaptability by focusing on intrinsic distribution differences, they suffer from a critical theoretical flaw in practice. 2ST-based detection relies on the null hypothesis that the unauthored text and the human-written text (HWT) reference come from the exact same distribution. This implies an assumption that the distributions of HWTs and MGTs are disjoint ($S_h \cap S_m = \emptyset$). In real-world scenarios, these distributions often overlap. Consequently, when a human-written text deviates slightly from the reference distribution (out-of-distribution HWT), the 2ST detector rejects the null hypothesis and incorrectly flags the text as machine-generated. This leads to an unacceptably high False Positive Rate (FPR), rendering such tools risky for sensitive applications like academic integrity verification.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose to fundamentally reframe the MGT detection task from a standard two-sample verification problem to a **Non-Parametric Kernel Relative Test** problem.

Our core hypothesis is that determining whether a text is "closer" to the distribution of human writings or machine writings is statistically more robust than determining if it belongs *exclusively* to the human distribution. By employing a Relative Test, we do not require the assumption that the target text belongs exclusively to either distribution. We hypothesize that this approach will:
1.  Significantly reduce False Positive Rates by accommodating HWTs that deviate from the reference samples.
2.  Maintain the zero-shot adaptability of non-parametric methods against new LLMs.

Furthermore, we hypothesize that the kernel function used in the relative test determines detection power. We propose to **optimize a Deep Kernel** by maximizing the test power of a surrogate two-sample test, thereby deriving a kernel that maximally separates HWT and MGT representations for use in the relative comparison.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework named **R-Detect** (Relative Test MGT Detection). This framework operates on textual representations and utilizes a statistical hypothesis test to classify content.

### 1. Problem Formulation and Text Space

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the space of all possible texts. We define the subspace of human-written texts as $\mathcal{S}_h \subset \mathcal{S}$ and machine-generated texts as $\mathcal{S}_m \subset \mathcal{S}$.
We define our detector $f$ as a composition $f = D \circ g$, where:
*   $g$: A fixed feature transformation function (e.g., a pre-trained transformer) converting text to representations.
*   $D$: A feature detector performing the statistical test.

### 2. The Relative Test Statistic

We will determine if a candidate text sample $Z_r$ (from distribution $\mathbb{Z}$) is closer to the human distribution $\mathbb{P}$ or the machine distribution $\mathbb{Q}$.
We assume we have access to independent reference observations:
*   Human References: $X_m := \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^m \sim \mathbb{P}^m$
*   Machine References: $Y_n := \{\mathbf{y}_j\}_{j=1}^n \sim \mathbb{Q}^n$
*   Target Text: $Z_r := \{\mathbf{z}_l\}_{l=1}^r \sim \mathbb{Z}^r$

We employ the **Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD)** as our distance metric. The unbiased empirical estimate of the squared MMD is defined as:

$$ \mathrm{MMD}_u^2(X_m, Y_n; k) = \frac{1}{m(m-1)} \sum_{i \neq j}^m h(\mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{v}_j) $$

where $h$ is the kernel core defined over observations $\mathbf{v}$:
$$ h(\mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{v}_j) = k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) - k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{y}_j) - k(\mathbf{y}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) + k(\mathbf{y}_i, \mathbf{y}_j) $$

The **Relative Test** formulates the following hypothesis:
*   **Null Hypothesis ($H_0$):** $\mathrm{MMD}(\mathbb{P}, \mathbb{Z}) \le \mathrm{MMD}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z})$ (The text is closer to, or equidistant to, Human distribution).
*   **Alternative Hypothesis ($H_1$):** $\mathrm{MMD}(\mathbb{P}, \mathbb{Z}) > \mathrm{MMD}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z})$ (The text is closer to Machine distribution).

We calculate the $p$-value for testing $H_0$ versus $H_1$ as:

$$ p \leq \Phi \left( - \frac{\mathrm{MMD}_u^2(X_m, Z_r; k) - \mathrm{MMD}_u^2(Y_n, Z_r; k)}{\sqrt{\sigma_{XZ}^2 + \sigma_{YZ}^2 - 2\sigma_{XZYZ}}} \right) $$

where:
*   $\Phi$ is the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution.
*   $\mathrm{MMD}_u^2(X_m, Z_r; k)$ measures distance between Human reference and Target.
*   $\mathrm{MMD}_u^2(Y_n, Z_r; k)$ measures distance between Machine reference and Target.
*   $\sigma^2$ terms represent the variances of the respective MMD estimators, and $\sigma_{XZYZ}$ is the covariance term (empirically estimated via kernel matrices).

**Decision Rule:** Given a significance level $\alpha$ (e.g., 0.05), we define the decision function $f(s)$ as:
$$ f(s) = \begin{cases} \mathbf{MGT} & \text{if } p < \alpha \\ \mathbf{HWT} & \text{if } p \ge \alpha \end{cases} $$

### 3. Deep Kernel Optimisation

The choice of kernel $k$ is critical. A simple Gaussian kernel is insufficient for complex textual data. We will implement a **Deep Kernel** parameterized by $\omega$, denoted as $k_\omega$.

**Architecture:**
The kernel is defined as a mixture of a deep neural network kernel and a standard Gaussian kernel:
$$ k_\omega(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = (1-\epsilon)\kappa(\phi_\omega(\mathbf{x}), \phi_\omega(\mathbf{x}')) + \epsilon q(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') $$
*   $\epsilon \in (0, 1)$ is a weighting parameter.
*   $\kappa$ and $q$ are Gaussian kernels with bandwidths $\sigma_\phi$ and $\sigma_q$.
*   $\phi_\omega$ is a deep neural network. Specifically, we will utilize a Transformer-based architecture followed by a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). The data flow will be: Input ($768d$) $\to$ Projector ($512d$) $\to$ MLP ($300d$).

**Optimization Strategy:**
We posit that a kernel optimized for a Two-Sample Test (discriminating $\mathbb{P}$ from $\mathbb{Q}$) will also perform optimally for the Relative Test. Therefore, we will optimize $\omega$ by maximizing the test power of the 2ST on a training set of historical HWTs and MGTs.

The objective function to maximize is the ratio of the MMD population estimate to its standard deviation (a proxy for test power):
$$ J_\omega(X, Y) = \frac{\mathrm{MMD}_u^2(X, Y; k_\omega)}{\sigma_{XY}(X, Y; k_\omega)} + \lambda \Omega(\omega) $$
We will optimize this using the Adam optimizer to learn the parameters $\omega$ that best separate the training distributions.

### 4. Implementation Details
*   **Feature Extraction ($g$):** We will fix $g$ as the OpenAI RoBERTa-based GPT-2 detector model (extracting the last hidden state) to convert raw text into dense vectors before passing them to the kernel.
*   **Data Handling:** The system requires no training on the target text itself, only on a reference set to learn the kernel parameters. This maintains the zero-shot capability.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Theoretical Advancement:** We expect to establish the Relative Test as a more rigorous statistical foundation for MGT detection than the prevailing Two-Sample Test, specifically addressing the "non-overlapping distribution" fallacy.
2.  **Accuracy & Robustness:** By determining relative similarity rather than absolute membership, we anticipate a significant reduction in False Positive Rates, particularly for human texts that are outliers in the standard distribution.
3.  **Kernel Methodology:** We will demonstrate that kernels optimized for discriminatory power in 2ST contexts can be directly transferred to empower Relative Tests, providing a novel method for kernel selection in this domain.
4.  **Practical Viability:** The proposed architecture will offer an interpretable, non-parametric solution that does not require access to the logits or probability distributions of the generator LLM, making it applicable to "black-box" API models.

agent.how: one sibling container (rwe-b1-agentic-scientist-agent:df83138) per agent session, started by the orchestrator

network.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
network.web_access: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

tools.permissions: upstream's own agent settings; provider web search denied by managed settings (Claude Code permissions.deny WebSearch, Codex web_search="disabled")

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no coding agent: a 23-stage prompt-chain pipeline over the Anthropic Messages API

network.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).

tools.permissions: no tool calls (requests carry model, messages, max_tokens); generated experiments run as plain subprocesses in the container

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
